sources.title: Contributions paid abroad can be combined with Irish contributions
sources.snippet: Ireland has social security arrangements with other countries that allow you to combine social insurance contributions that you have paid in Ireland with social insurance contributions that you have paid in another country. This can help you to qualify for a social insurance payment in Ireland or in a country with whom Ireland has a social security arrangement.

sources.title: PRSI is compulsory for most employees between 16 and pensionable age
sources.snippet: Most employers and employees (between the ages of 16 and pensionable age, currently 66* years) pay social insurance (PRSI) contributions into the SIF. In general, the payment of PRSI is compulsory. Most employees are liable to pay Class A PRSI.

sources.title: The employer's RPN drives Income Tax, USC and PRSI deductions
sources.snippet: Revenue will make a Revenue Payroll Notification (RPN) available to your employer when you have registered your job with Revenue. When your employer obtains the RPN they can calculate the correct deductions of: Income Tax; Universal Social Charge (USC); and Pay Related Social Insurance (PRSI).

sources.title: Irish tax residence turns on 183 days in a year, or 280 across two
sources.snippet: You are resident in Ireland for tax purposes if you are present in Ireland for: 183 days or more in a tax year; or 280 days or more in total, taking the current tax year plus the preceding tax year together. You will not be resident in Ireland if you are here for 30 days or less in a tax year.

sources.title: Register the job with Revenue through myAccount to avoid emergency tax
sources.snippet: When you start your first job, you should notify Revenue as soon as possible, or you may have to pay Emergency Tax. To do this, you need to register for myAccount. Once registered for myAccount you can register your job by clicking 'Add Job or Pension Details' under the 'PAYE Services' tab. When you have registered your first job, Revenue will make a Revenue Payroll Notification (RPN) available to your new employer.

sources.title: A PPS number is required for employment and tax administration
sources.snippet: If you are aged 18 years or older you can apply for a PPS Number for yourself and your child online at MyWelfare. This service is available to customers resident on the island of Ireland and customers resident abroad. To apply for a PPS Number, you must provide: evidence of your identity; evidence of your address; The reason why you need a PPSN.

sources.title: Proof of address for a PPS application must be under three months old
sources.snippet: The document must show your name and address and not be older than 3 months. You can use any of the following documents to do this: household utility bill; an official letter or document; a bank statement; property lease or tenancy agreement; official letter from a Government department or agency; official confirmation of address by a third party.

sources.title: Split-year treatment can be requested for the year of arrival
sources.snippet: You can request split-year treatment on your employment income for the year you move to Ireland if: you are resident in Ireland in that year; you are not resident in Ireland in the previous year; and you are going to be resident in Ireland in the year following your arrival here. Split-year treatment applies to employment income only. Employment income you earned abroad in that year before you arrived in Ireland is ignored for Irish tax purposes.

sources.title: Emergency tax applies until the job is registered, rising to 40% from week five
sources.snippet: If you have provided your PPSN to your employer, but your job has not been registered with Revenue, your employer will be unable to obtain an RPN for you. Your employer will be obliged to apply the below Emergency Tax rules on your gross pay. Where you have provided your PPSN, you are allowed a single person’s rate band for the first four weeks of employment. From Week 5 onwards, your full income will be taxed at the higher rate (40%).

content.overview: Dublin's rental market is very tight and moves in days, not weeks. Daft.ie's Q1 2026 report puts the Dublin average at EUR 2,012 for a 1-bed and EUR 2,609 for a 2-bed; by sub-market a 2-bed runs about EUR 2,850 in the South City and EUR 2,444 in the North City. Viewings are often group slots — bring ID, proof of employment and references ready to send the same day.

content.overview: State primary and secondary schools are free, but most are managed by a patron body and many are heavily oversubscribed in Dublin — apply as early as you can. International schools charge fees and are limited in number.

Healthcare in Ireland is not free at the point of use for most workers. On a professional salary you will not qualify for a medical card (the single-person means limit is about EUR 184/week), so expect to pay EUR 45–65 per GP visit — fees are unregulated and vary by practice. Many Dublin practices are closed to new patients, so register early. Employer health insurance is common and worth activating before you arrive.

content.overview: Dublin runs on buses, the DART coastal rail line and two Luas tram lines; there is no metro. A Leap Card is the cheapest way to pay and caps your spend automatically. Traffic is heavy and city-centre parking is expensive, so most commuters do not drive in.

content.overview: Mobile and broadband are competitive and mostly contract-free if you prefer. Electricity and gas are self-arranged and you can switch supplier freely; bin collection is a private contract you arrange yourself, which surprises most new arrivals.

content.overview: Dublin has large Spanish, Brazilian, Polish and Indian communities and an active meetup culture. Sports clubs (GAA, rugby, running) are the usual route into a local network.
National museums and the National Gallery are free. The city is walkable, and the coast is on the DART line in both directions.

Phoenix Park is one of Europe's largest enclosed city parks. The Dublin and Wicklow mountains start about 40 minutes south, and Howth and Bray offer coastal cliff walks reachable by DART without a car.
Dublin is expensive by EU standards and rent dominates the budget. Figures below are Dublin-wide averages; see the housing section for sub-market variation.

recommended.title: Utilities, broadband and bin collection
recommended.summary: Energy and broadband are switchable; refuse collection is a private contract you arrange.
recommended.body: Electricity and gas are arranged by you directly and you can switch supplier freely, so comparing prices is worthwhile. Broadband is competitive and widely available in Dublin. The detail that catches most new arrivals is refuse: household bin collection is not a council service you inherit with the property but a private contract you arrange yourself with an operator.

recommended.title: Emergency numbers and the EUR 100 ED charge
recommended.summary: 112 and 999 both work. Attending ED without a GP referral costs EUR 100.
recommended.body: Both 112 and 999 reach the emergency services in Ireland. Attending a hospital emergency department without a referral from a GP carries a charge of EUR 100 per visit; the charge does not apply if your GP has referred you, which is another reason to register with a practice early.

recommended.title: Healthcare is not free at the point of use
recommended.summary: Expect EUR 45–65 per GP visit; a professional salary will not qualify for a medical card.
recommended.body: Ireland does not provide free general practice to most workers. The medical card that covers GP visits is means tested, and with a single-person income limit around EUR 184 per week a professional salary will not qualify. GP fees are unregulated and typically fall between EUR 45 and EUR 65 per consultation. Many employers provide private health insurance, which is worth activating before you arrive rather than after.

recommended.title: Residence registration — what applies to you depends on your nationality
recommended.summary: EEA and Swiss citizens register nothing. Non-EEA nationals get an IRP within 90 days.
recommended.body: If you are an EU, EEA or Swiss citizen you do not register with the immigration authorities at all and you do not need a residence card to live in Ireland — there is no equivalent of a German Anmeldung or a Norwegian folkeregister step. If you are a non-EEA national you must register and obtain an Irish Residence Permit within 90 days of arrival; first-time registration is done at Burgh Quay in Dublin, costs EUR 300, and an employment-permit holder is normally granted Stamp 1.

recommended.title: Step 3 — Open an Irish bank account
recommended.summary: Banks want photo ID plus a separate proof of address — plan the order.
recommended.body: Irish banks ask for photo identification and, separately, evidence of your Irish address. This is where new arrivals get stuck: you will not yet have a utility bill in your name, and an EEA citizen never receives an Irish Residence Permit to use as a document. Correspondence issued after your PPSN and Revenue registration is usually the first acceptable address evidence you hold, which is why the PPSN and Revenue steps come first.

requirements.label: Critical Skills Permit – salary threshold
requirements.description: Critical Skills Employment Permit requires a minimum annual remuneration of €40,904 (based on a 39-hour week; €41,953.60 for a 40-hour week), rising further under the published MAR roadmap.

requirements.label: Dublin rental market — practical realities
requirements.description:
Most rentals are advertised on accommodation websites, where you can search and set up alerts for your requirements.
Rentals are usually let on a fixed-term tenancy covering a set period, for example 6 months or a year or more.
If you sign one lease together with others (a joint tenancy), each tenant is responsible for ALL the rent — you can be liable for the whole amount if a housemate does not pay.
The private rental market in Ireland is tight and it can be difficult to find accommodation, especially in Dublin.

requirements.label: Immigration permission – CSEP to Stamp 4
requirements.description: After holding a valid Critical Skills Employment Permit for 2 years, the holder may apply directly to the Department of Justice for a Stamp 4 immigration permission, which grants unrestricted access to the labour market without requiring a further employment permit.

requirements.label: Immigration permission – Stamp 1 / IRP registration
requirements.description: Non-EEA employment permit holders intending to stay in Ireland for more than 90 days must register their immigration permission (Stamp 1) with Immigration Service Delivery and obtain an Irish Residence Permit (IRP); registration must occur promptly after arrival.

requirements.label: General Employment Permit – application fee
requirements.description: The processing fee for a General Employment Permit is €1,500 for a permit of 6 months up to 36 months duration; the renewal fee is €1,500 for up to 36 months.

requirements.label: General Employment Permit – Labour Market Needs Test
requirements.description: General Employment Permit applications require a Labour Market Needs Test (LMNT) in most cases: the employer must advertise the vacancy on EURES for at least 28 consecutive days (plus JobsIreland.ie and one other platform) before submitting a valid application.

requirements.label: Bringing a pet from Spain to Ireland — EU pet travel rules
requirements.description:
Because Spain is an EU country, you follow the EU pet travel steps to bring your cat, dog or ferret to Ireland.
Your pet must be microchipped BEFORE it is vaccinated against rabies — the order is mandatory and cannot be reversed.
A rabies vaccination is required after microchipping; the pet must be at least 12 weeks old when it is vaccinated.
For dogs, a vet must give a tapeworm treatment between 1 and 5 days before you arrive in Ireland, recorded in the pet passport.
You need an EU pet passport (issued by an EU country) to bring the pet into Ireland.

requirements.label: IRP card — first-time registration timeline and fee
requirements.description:
Non-EEA nationals (from outside the EU, EEA, UK or Switzerland) who intend to reside in Ireland for more than 90 days must register their immigration permission with Immigration Service Delivery (ISD).
You must register your immigration permission within 90 days of arriving in Ireland.
After you register, your IRP card is posted to the address you provide; you should receive it within 10 working days.
The first-time registration fee is €300 per person (where applicable) and can be paid by credit or debit card only.

requirements.label: Critical Skills Employment Permit — eligibility
requirements.description: Non-EEA nationals (e.g. Indian nationals) must hold a qualifying job offer of at least 2 years from an Irish-registered employer in a role on the Critical Skills Occupations List to apply for a Critical Skills Employment Permit (CSEP).

requirements.label: General Employment Permit – salary threshold
requirements.description: General Employment Permit requires a minimum annual remuneration of €36,605 (39-hour week; €37,544 for a 40-hour week) following the March 2026 increase under the government's MAR roadmap.

requirements.label: Critical Skills Permit – application fee
requirements.description: The processing fee for a Critical Skills Employment Permit is €1,000. If the application is unsuccessful, 90% of the fee (€900) is refunded to the applicant.

requirements.label: Ireland outside the Schengen area — separate immigration system
requirements.description:
An Irish Residence Permit (IRP) does not by itself allow Schengen travel — a non-EEA resident of Ireland may need a separate Schengen visa to visit Schengen countries.
A Schengen visa does not admit you to Ireland — non-EEA nationals may need a separate Irish visa even if they hold a Schengen visa.
Ireland is not part of the Schengen Area, so travelling between Ireland and Schengen countries means passing through an immigration checkpoint with your passport or national ID.

requirements.label: PPSN (Personal Public Service Number) — application and emergency tax
requirements.description:
You apply for a PPSN online at MyWelfare (mywelfare.ie); the online service is for people living in Ireland who are 18 or over.
If you start work before your PPSN and job are registered with Revenue, your employer must tax all your pay at the higher emergency rate of 40% until your tax record is set up.
On top of income tax, an emergency Universal Social Charge (USC) applies as a flat rate (8% in 2026) on all income while you are on the emergency basis.
A PPSN is the unique identifier you need to access employment, tax, social welfare, public services and government information in Ireland; anyone taking up work needs one.

requirements.label: Critical Skills Permit – occupation list
requirements.description: For a Critical Skills Employment Permit, the role must appear on the Critical Skills Occupations List (Schedule 3 of the Regulations, updated by SI 213 of 2026, effective 13 May 2026). Roles earning €68,911 or more annually are generally eligible regardless of occupation.

sources.snippet: Most employers and employees (between the ages of 16 and pensionable age, currently 66* years) pay social insurance (PRSI) contributions into the SIF. In general, the payment of PRSI is compulsory. Most employees are liable to pay Class A PRSI.

sources.title: The employer's RPN drives Income Tax, USC and PRSI deductions
sources.snippet: Revenue will make a Revenue Payroll Notification (RPN) available to your employer when you have registered your job with Revenue. When your employer obtains the RPN they can calculate the correct deductions of: Income Tax; Universal Social Charge (USC); and Pay Related Social Insurance (PRSI).

sources.title: Irish tax residence turns on 183 days in a year, or 280 across two
sources.snippet: You are resident in Ireland for tax purposes if you are present in Ireland for: 183 days or more in a tax year; or 280 days or more in total, taking the current tax year plus the preceding tax year together. You will not be resident in Ireland if you are here for 30 days or less in a tax year.

sources.title: Register the job with Revenue through myAccount to avoid emergency tax
sources.snippet: When you start your first job, you should notify Revenue as soon as possible, or you may have to pay Emergency Tax. To do this, you need to register for myAccount. Once registered for myAccount you can register your job by clicking 'Add Job or Pension Details' under the 'PAYE Services' tab. When you have registered your first job, Revenue will make a Revenue Payroll Notification (RPN) available to your new employer.

sources.title: A PPS number is required for employment and tax administration
sources.snippet: If you are aged 18 years or older you can apply for a PPS Number for yourself and your child online at MyWelfare. This service is available to customers resident on the island of Ireland and customers resident abroad. To apply for a PPS Number, you must provide: evidence of your identity; evidence of your address; The reason why you need a PPSN.

sources.title: Proof of address for a PPS application must be under three months old
sources.snippet: The document must show your name and address and not be older than 3 months. You can use any of the following documents to do this: household utility bill; an official letter or document; a bank statement; property lease or tenancy agreement; official letter from a Government department or agency; official confirmation of address by a third party.

sources.title: Split-year treatment can be requested for the year of arrival
sources.snippet: You can request split-year treatment on your employment income for the year you move to Ireland if: you are resident in Ireland in that year; you are not resident in Ireland in the previous year; and you are going to be resident in Ireland in the year following your arrival here. Split-year treatment applies to employment income only. Employment income you earned abroad in that year before you arrived in Ireland is ignored for Irish tax purposes.

sources.title: Emergency tax applies until the job is registered, rising to 40% from week five
sources.snippet: If you have provided your PPSN to your employer, but your job has not been registered with Revenue, your employer will be unable to obtain an RPN for you. Your employer will be obliged to apply the below Emergency Tax rules on your gross pay. Where you have provided your PPSN, you are allowed a single person’s rate band for the first four weeks of employment. From Week 5 onwards, your full income will be taxed at the higher rate (40%).

content.overview: Dublin's rental market is very tight and moves in days, not weeks. Daft.ie's Q1 2026 report puts the Dublin average at EUR 2,012 for a 1-bed and EUR 2,609 for a 2-bed; by sub-market a 2-bed runs about EUR 2,850 in the South City and EUR 2,444 in the North City. Viewings are often group slots — bring ID, proof of employment and references ready to send the same day.

Drumcondra — quieter northside, good value, near Croke Park

content.overview: State primary and secondary schools are free, but most are managed by a patron body and many are heavily oversubscribed in Dublin — apply as early as you can. International schools charge fees and are limited in number.

Healthcare in Ireland is not free at the point of use for most workers. On a professional salary you will not qualify for a medical card (the single-person means limit is about EUR 184/week), so expect to pay EUR 45–65 per GP visit — fees are unregulated and vary by practice. Many Dublin practices are closed to new patients, so register early. Employer health insurance is common and worth activating before you arrive.

items.title: Emergency numbers and the EUR 100 ED charge
items.summary: 112 and 999 both work. Attending ED without a GP referral costs EUR 100.

content.overview: Dublin runs on buses, the DART coastal rail line and two Luas tram lines; there is no metro. A Leap Card is the cheapest way to pay and caps your spend automatically. Traffic is heavy and city-centre parking is expensive, so most commuters do not drive in.

content.overview: Dublin has large Spanish, Brazilian, Polish and Indian communities and an active meetup culture. Sports clubs (GAA, rugby, running) are the usual route into a local network.
National museums and the National Gallery are free. The city is walkable, and the coast is on the DART line in both directions.

Phoenix Park is one of Europe's largest enclosed city parks. The Dublin and Wicklow mountains start about 40 minutes south, and Howth and Bray offer coastal cliff walks reachable by DART without a car.
Dublin is expensive by EU standards and rent dominates the budget. Figures below are Dublin-wide averages; see the housing section for sub-market variation.

recommended.title: Utilities, broadband and bin collection
recommended.summary: Energy and broadband are switchable; refuse collection is a private contract you arrange.
recommended.body: Electricity and gas are arranged by you directly and you can switch supplier freely, so comparing prices is worthwhile. Broadband is competitive and widely available in Dublin. The detail that catches most new arrivals is refuse: household bin collection is not a council service you inherit with the property but a private contract you arrange yourself with an operator.

recommended.title: Emergency numbers and the EUR 100 ED charge
recommended.summary: 112 and 999 both work. Attending ED without a GP referral costs EUR 100.
recommended.body: Both 112 and 999 reach the emergency services in Ireland. Attending a hospital emergency department without a referral from a GP carries a charge of EUR 100 per visit; the charge does not apply if your GP has referred you, which is another reason to register with a practice early.

recommended.title: Healthcare is not free at the point of use
recommended.summary: Expect EUR 45–65 per GP visit; a professional salary will not qualify for a medical card.
recommended.body: Ireland does not provide free general practice to most workers. The medical card that covers GP visits is means tested, and with a single-person income limit around EUR 184 per week a professional salary will not qualify. GP fees are unregulated and typically fall between EUR 45 and EUR 65 per consultation. Many employers provide private health insurance, which is worth activating before you arrive rather than after.

recommended.title: Residence registration — what applies to you depends on your nationality
recommended.summary: EEA and Swiss citizens register nothing. Non-EEA nationals get an IRP within 90 days.
recommended.body: If you are an EU, EEA or Swiss citizen you do not register with the immigration authorities at all and you do not need a residence card to live in Ireland — there is no equivalent of a German Anmeldung or a Norwegian folkeregister step. If you are a non-EEA national you must register and obtain an Irish Residence Permit within 90 days of arrival; first-time registration is done at Burgh Quay in Dublin, costs EUR 300, and an employment-permit holder is normally granted Stamp 1.

recommended.title: Step 3 — Open an Irish bank account
recommended.summary: Banks want photo ID plus a separate proof of address — plan the order.
recommended.body: Irish banks ask for photo identification and, separately, evidence of your Irish address. This is where new arrivals get stuck: you will not yet have a utility bill in your name, and an EEA citizen never receives an Irish Residence Permit to use as a document. Correspondence issued after your PPSN and Revenue registration is usually the first acceptable address evidence you hold, which is why the PPSN and Revenue steps come first.
